EXCLUDED = {"ColombiaPrimeraA", "ColombiaPrimeraB", "EnglandLeague2"}  # no league/tier context yet

qa = load("corner_adj_qa_summary.csv")

::: {.lede}
Corner betting markets rate teams on how many corners they win and concede. But
the number of corners a team takes depends a lot on the scoreline and on how
strong the opponent is, and over a short run of fixtures those two things
skew the raw counts. This project removes that bias by valuing
every corner in the context it was won, builds team ratings from the adjusted
values, and tests them against Pinnacle's corner prices.
:::

::: {.stat-row}
::: {.stat}

:::

**The short version:**

- Game state has a large effect on corners. In the median league, the home side's share of
  corners is `{python} f"{med_spread:.0f}"` points higher when trailing than when leading.
- Over short periods, teams spend much more or much less time leading or trailing than
  their strength would suggest, so raw corner counts are a noisy measure of ability.
- Valuing each corner by its game state, its home/away context and the pre-match
  supremacy, and dropping "repeater" corners, gives ratings that predict
  future corners better than raw counts do at every window length tested.
- Against real Pinnacle prices, the adjusted ratings are profitable in the
  **corner handicap market** (all `{python} n_combos` rating sets tested,
  `{python} n_bets_lo`–`{python} n_bets_hi` bets each). They show **no edge in
  corner totals**, which lost money in every configuration.

## 1. The data

Event data (goals, corners and cards, with the minute of each) is scraped from
totalcorner.com, along with Pinnacle's pre-match Asian handicap and goal lines.
From those two lines I back out each match's expected goals and
**supremacy** (the expected goal difference), which gives a market-implied
measure of how strong each team is going in.

The original study covered seven top-flight European leagues from 2014–2025. The
production model now covers `{python} n_leagues` leagues across 1st and 2nd
tiers. The league comparison in section 2, the league explorer in section 5 and
sections 7–8 use the full model. The worked examples (Premier League, La Liga and
the case study) use the original seven-league data.

Here is one match as raw events, with the running score and game state added
(0 = level, 1 = home leading, 2 = away leading):

```{python}
ev = load("example_match_events.csv")
ev.columns = ["Minute", "Team", "Event", "Home goals", "Away goals", "Game state"]
table(ev, floatfmt=".0f")
```

From the state changes we can work out how long each team spent in each state,
and which state each corner was won in:

```{python}
table(load("example_match_minutes.csv"), floatfmt=".0f")
```

## 2. Game state drives corner share

Teams that are behind attack more, so they win more corners. Teams that are
ahead sit deeper and win fewer. The chart shows the home side's share of all corners
in each league, split by the scoreline at the time.

```{python}
share = load("gs_home_corner_share.csv")
share = share[~share["League"].isin(EXCLUDED)]
p = share.assign(League=share["League"].map(pretty_league)).pivot(index="League", columns="home_match_state", values="home_share_pct")
p["spread"] = p["trailing"] - p["leading"]
p = p.sort_values("spread")

fig = go.Figure()
for league in p.index:  # connector line per league
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[p.loc[league, "leading"], p.loc[league, "trailing"]], y=[league, league],
                             mode="lines", line=dict(color="#d8d7d2", width=2),
                             showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip"))
for col, label in [("leading", "Leading"), ("level", "Level"), ("trailing", "Trailing")]:
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=p[col], y=p.index, mode="markers", name=f"Home {label.lower()}",
        marker=dict(size=9, color=STATE_COLORS[label], line=dict(color="white", width=1.5)),
        customdata=p["spread"],
        hovertemplate=f"<b>%{{y}}</b><br>Home {label.lower()}: %{{x:.1f}}%<br>Trailing − leading: %{{customdata:.1f}} pts<extra></extra>",
    ))
fig.add_vline(x=50, line=dict(color=MUTED, width=1, dash="dot"))
fig.update_layout(height=26 * len(p) + 90, title="Home share of corners (%) by scoreline",
                  xaxis=dict(title=None, ticksuffix="%"), yaxis=dict(title=None, dtick=1, tickfont=dict(size=11)))
show(fig)
```

The size of the effect varies a lot by league: from about
`{python} f"{p['spread'].min():.0f}"` points in `{python} p['spread'].idxmin()` to
`{python} f"{p['spread'].max():.0f}"` points in `{python} p['spread'].idxmax()`.
Tactical culture, home-crowd effects and how often a league's favourites dominate all play a part.
**Any adjustment has to be league-specific.**

## 3. Short runs of games distort the picture

If every team spent a predictable amount of time in each state, game state
would wash out of the ratings. Over short samples it doesn't. The left panel
shows how long each Premier League side *should* have spent leading,
level and trailing over the first nine games of 2023/24, based on the pre-match lines.
The right panel shows how long they actually did.

```{python}
m = load("epl_2324_state_minutes.csv")
exp = m[m["basis"] == "Expected"].sort_values("Leading")
order = exp["Team"].tolist()
act = m[m["basis"] == "Actual"].set_index("Team").loc[order].reset_index()

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, shared_yaxes=True, horizontal_spacing=0.04,
                    subplot_titles=("Expected (from betting lines)", "Actual"))
for col_i, df_ in enumerate([exp, act], start=1):
    for state in ["Leading", "Level", "Trailing"]:
        fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
            y=df_["Team"], x=df_[state], orientation="h", name=state,
            marker=dict(color=STATE_COLORS[state], line=dict(color="white", width=1)),
            legendgroup=state, showlegend=(col_i == 1),
            hovertemplate=f"<b>%{{y}}</b><br>{state}: %{{x:.0%}}<extra></extra>",
        ), row=1, col=col_i)
fig.update_layout(barmode="stack", height=560, bargap=0.2)
fig.update_xaxes(tickformat=".0%", range=[0, 1], dtick=0.25)
fig.update_annotations(font=dict(size=13, color=TEXT_2))
show(fig)
```

Nine games is roughly the sample a market has to go on early in a season. Over that stretch,
several teams spent far more or far less time trailing than their strength
implied. Their raw corner numbers are inflated or deflated as a result, and the
next opponent doesn't inherit that game state.

## 4. Repeaters

A **repeater** is a corner that follows another corner by the same team, in
the same half, within a minute: the ball goes straight back out off a defender. Runs of
three or four in a row are common. They aren't independent events, so they add noise.

```{python}
rep = load("repeaters_by_league.csv")
rep_team = load("repeaters_by_team.csv")
t = rep[["League", "corners", "repeaters", "repeater_rate"]].copy()
t["repeater_rate"] = (t["repeater_rate"] * 100).round(1).astype(str) + "%"
t.columns = ["League", "Corners", "Repeaters", "Repeater rate"]
table(t)
```

```{python}
rt = rep_team.sort_values("League")
fig = go.Figure(go.Box(
    x=rt["repeater_rate"], y=rt["League"], orientation="h", boxpoints="all", jitter=0.4, pointpos=0,
    marker=dict(color=ACCENT, size=6, opacity=0.6), line=dict(color=MUTED, width=1), fillcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    customdata=rt[["Team", "matches"]],
    hovertemplate="<b>%{customdata[0]}</b><br>Repeater rate: %{x:.1%}<br>Matches: %{customdata[1]}<extra></extra>",
    showlegend=False))
fig.update_layout(title="Repeater rate by team (teams with 50+ matches)", height=380,
                  xaxis=dict(tickformat=".0%"), yaxis=dict(title=None))
show(fig)
```

The rate is stable at around 13–15% across leagues and across teams within each league, so
removing repeaters doesn't penalise any particular style of play. It just removes
correlated noise. In the full `{python} n_leagues`-league model the league range is
`{python} f"{qa['repeater_rate'].min():.1f}"`–`{python} f"{qa['repeater_rate'].max():.1f}"`%.

## 5. Supremacy matters in every game state

Stronger teams win more corners, and that holds whether they're leading, level or
trailing. To measure it, each La Liga team-match is put into one of 30 equal-sized
supremacy buckets. Within each bucket I calculate corners per minute for each
game state, then fit a line per state, separately for home and away sides.

```{python}
b = load("laliga_sup_buckets.csv")
name_map = {"Winning": "Leading", "Drawing": "Level", "Losing": "Trailing"}
b["state"] = b["game_state"].map(name_map)

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, shared_yaxes=True, horizontal_spacing=0.05, subplot_titles=("Home", "Away"))
for col_i, side in enumerate(["Home", "Away"], start=1):
    for state in ["Leading", "Level", "Trailing"]:
        d = b[(b["side"] == side) & (b["state"] == state)]
        slope, intercept = np.polyfit(d["sup_mean"], d["cpm"], 1)
        xs = np.array([d["sup_mean"].min(), d["sup_mean"].max()])
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=d["sup_mean"], y=d["cpm"], mode="markers", name=state, legendgroup=state, showlegend=(col_i == 1),
            marker=dict(color=STATE_COLORS[state], size=8, opacity=0.75, line=dict(color="white", width=1)),
            customdata=d[["corners", "mins"]],
            hovertemplate=f"{side} · {state}<br>Supremacy %{{x:.2f}}<br>%{{y:.3f}} corners/min<br>%{{customdata[0]:,}} corners in %{{customdata[1]:,.0f}} mins<extra></extra>",
        ), row=1, col=col_i)
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=xs, y=intercept + slope * xs, mode="lines", legendgroup=state, showlegend=False,
                                 line=dict(color=STATE_COLORS[state], width=2), hoverinfo="skip"), row=1, col=col_i)
fig.update_layout(height=440, title="La Liga: corners per minute vs pre-match supremacy")
fig.update_xaxes(title="Team supremacy (goals)")
fig.update_yaxes(title="Corners per minute", row=1, col=1)
fig.update_annotations(font=dict(size=13, color=TEXT_2))
show(fig)
```

These six lines give an *expected* corner rate for any combination of home/away,
game state and supremacy. The full model fits the same six lines for every league.
The chart below lets you pick any league.

```{python}
co = load("gs_coefficients.csv")
co = co[~co["League"].isin(EXCLUDED)]
co["League"] = co["League"].map(pretty_league)
state_code = {0: "Level", 1: "Leading", 2: "Trailing"}
xs = np.linspace(-2, 2, 21)
leagues = sorted(co["League"].unique())
default = "Spain La Liga"

fig = go.Figure()
for lg in leagues:
    for _, r in co[co["League"] == lg].iterrows():
        st = state_code[r["team_gamestate"]]
        home = r["home_status"] == "home"
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=xs, y=r["Intercept"] + r["Coefficient"] * xs, mode="lines",
            name=f"{st} ({'home' if home else 'away'})", visible=(lg == default),
            line=dict(color=STATE_COLORS[st], width=2, dash="solid" if home else "dash"),
            hovertemplate=f"{st}, {'home' if home else 'away'}<br>Supremacy %{{x:.1f}}: %{{y:.3f}} corners/min<extra></extra>",
        ))
per = len(fig.data) // len(leagues)
buttons = [dict(label=lg, method="update",
                args=[{"visible": [i // per == j for i in range(len(fig.data))]}])
           for j, lg in enumerate(leagues)]
fig.update_layout(
    height=440, title="Fitted corner rate by league (solid = home, dashed = away)",
    updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, active=leagues.index(default), x=0, xanchor="left", y=1.02, yanchor="bottom",
                      bgcolor="white", bordercolor="#d8d7d2")],
    xaxis=dict(title="Team supremacy (goals)"), yaxis=dict(title="Corners per minute", rangemode="tozero"),
    legend=dict(y=-0.22, yanchor="top"),
)
show(fig)
```

## 6. Adjusted corner values

Each corner is valued as the *average* corner rate divided by the rate we'd
*expect* given the context it was won in:

$$
\text{value} = \frac{\text{average rate}_{\text{home/away}}}{\text{expected rate}(\text{home/away},\ \text{game state},\ \text{supremacy})}
$$

A corner won where corners are usually rare (a big underdog, while leading) is worth
more than 1. One won where they're usually plentiful (a big favourite chasing the game)
is worth less than 1. Repeaters are worth 0.

**Case study: Rayo Vallecano 1–2 Barcelona, 27 August 2024.** Barcelona went in
as 0.77-goal favourites. Rayo scored in the 9th minute, Barcelona equalised in the 60th
and won it with an 82nd-minute goal.

```{python}
cs = load("case_study_corners.csv")
cs["team_state"] = cs["team_state"].map(name_map)
cs["Repeater"] = cs["Repeater"].map({0: "", 1: "yes"})
tbl = cs[["Minute", "Team", "team_state", "Repeater", "expected_rate", "avg_rate", "adj_corner_value"]].copy()
tbl.columns = ["Min", "Team", "Team state", "Repeater", "Expected rate", "Average rate", "Value"]
table(tbl, floatfmt=".3f")
```

```{python}
tot = cs.groupby("Team").agg(raw=("Minute", "size"), adj=("adj_corner_value", "sum"))
rv, ba = tot.loc["Rayo Vallecano"], tot.loc["Barcelona"]
```

- **Level:** Rayo corners are worth
  `{python} f"{cs[(cs.Team=='Rayo Vallecano')&(cs.team_state=='Level')].adj_corner_value.max():.2f}"` and
  Barcelona's `{python} f"{cs[(cs.Team=='Barcelona')&(cs.team_state=='Level')&(cs.Repeater=='')].adj_corner_value.max():.2f}"`.
  The gap reflects the difference in team strength alone.
- **Rayo leading:** a Rayo corner is worth
  `{python} f"{cs[(cs.Team=='Rayo Vallecano')&(cs.team_state=='Leading')].adj_corner_value.max():.2f}"`,
  because an underdog sitting on a lead rarely wins corners. Barcelona's are
  worth `{python} f"{cs[(cs.Team=='Barcelona')&(cs.team_state=='Trailing')].adj_corner_value.max():.2f}"`,
  because a favourite chasing the game is expected to win lots of them.
- **Barcelona leading:** the game-state and supremacy effects roughly cancel out,
  and both sides' corners are worth close to 1.

Raw corners: **`{python} f"{rv.raw:.0f}"`–`{python} f"{ba.raw:.0f}"`**. Adjusted:
**`{python} f"{rv.adj:.2f}"`–`{python} f"{ba.adj:.2f}"`**. Once you account for Barcelona
chasing the game for more than 50 minutes and three repeaters are removed,
Rayo's corner performance looks clearly better than Barcelona's.

```{python}
code_link("code/adjusted_values.py", "Buckets, fitted lines and adjusted values")
```

Because supremacy is stripped out of each corner's value, a team's rating no
longer depends much on *who* it has played. That means shorter rating windows
can be used, so changes of manager or personnel show up sooner. It also means
promoted and relegated teams carry their ratings between divisions without
special handling. The prediction model then adds supremacy back in as a separate
input, taken from the upcoming match's betting lines.

## 7. Do adjusted ratings predict better?

Team attack and defence ratings are built as rolling averages over the last
*N* games, using four metrics:

- **raw**: raw corner counts
- **nr**: raw counts with repeaters removed
- **adj**: adjusted values
- **adj_nr**: adjusted values with repeaters removed

Each set of ratings, together with match supremacy, feeds an OLS model that predicts each
side's corners in held-out matches. The chart shows the out-of-sample R²
improvement over raw counts, for each window length.

```{python}
piv = rb.pivot_table(index=["side", "window_size"], columns="metric", values="r2_test").reset_index()
for mt in ["nr", "adj", "adj_nr"]:
    piv[f"d_{mt}"] = (piv[mt] / piv["raw"] - 1) * 100

metric_colors = {"nr": MUTED, "adj": "#86b6ef", "adj_nr": ACCENT}
fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, shared_yaxes=True, horizontal_spacing=0.05,
                    subplot_titles=("Home corners", "Away corners"))
for col_i, side in enumerate(["home", "away"], start=1):
    d = piv[piv["side"] == side]
    for mt in ["nr", "adj", "adj_nr"]:
        fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
            x=d["window_size"].astype(str), y=d[f"d_{mt}"], name=mt, legendgroup=mt, showlegend=(col_i == 1),
            marker=dict(color=metric_colors[mt]),
            customdata=np.c_[d[mt], d["raw"]],
            hovertemplate=f"{mt}, window %{{x}}<br>R² %{{customdata[0]:.4f}} vs raw %{{customdata[1]:.4f}}<br>%{{y:+.1f}}% vs raw<extra></extra>",
        ), row=1, col=col_i)
fig.update_layout(barmode="group", height=400, title="Out-of-sample R², % change vs raw corner ratings")
fig.update_xaxes(title="Rating window (games)")
fig.update_yaxes(ticksuffix="%", zeroline=True, zerolinecolor=MUTED, row=1, col=1)
fig.update_annotations(font=dict(size=13, color=TEXT_2))
show(fig)

best = rb[(rb["metric"] == "adj_nr") & (rb["window_size"] == 25)].set_index("side")
raw25 = rb[(rb["metric"] == "raw") & (rb["window_size"] == 25)].set_index("side")
```

The adjusted metrics beat raw counts at every window length on both sides. The
gain is largest for home corners, which are the most sensitive to game state.
Removing repeaters from raw counts (nr) makes little difference on its own; almost
all of the gain comes from the game-state and supremacy adjustment. The
setting carried forward is **adj_nr over a 25-game window**, the strongest overall
(adj is level with it on home corners): home R²
`{python} f"{best.loc['home','r2_test']:.3f}"` vs `{python} f"{raw25.loc['home','r2_test']:.3f}"` raw, and away
`{python} f"{best.loc['away','r2_test']:.3f}"` vs `{python} f"{raw25.loc['away','r2_test']:.3f}"`.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
R² values of around 0.1 are normal here. Match-level corner counts are
dominated by Poisson-like randomness, so no pre-match model explains most of the
variance. What matters for betting is whether the model beats the market's
estimate, which is tested next.
:::

## 8. Does it beat the market?

The model's predicted corner supremacy (home minus away) is compared with
Pinnacle's implied corner supremacy for every priced match in 2024/25 and
2025/26. The prediction model is fitted only on earlier seasons, and ratings use only
matches played before each fixture. When the two differ by
0.5 corners or more, a 1-unit bet goes on the side the model prefers, at
Pinnacle's price. Every bet is settled on actual raw corners.

```{python}
bg = bets_g.copy()
bg["combo"] = bg["metric"] + " · " + bg["window_size"].astype(str)
bg = bg.sort_values("roi")
fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(
    x=bg["roi"], y=bg["combo"], orientation="h",
    marker=dict(color=np.where(bg["roi"] >= 0, POS, NEG)),
    customdata=bg[["n_bets", "total_pnl"]],
    text=(bg["roi"] * 100).map("{:+.1f}%".format), textposition="outside", textfont=dict(color=TEXT_2),
    hovertemplate="<b>%{y}</b><br>ROI %{x:.2%}<br>%{customdata[0]:,} bets · %{customdata[1]:+.1f} units<extra></extra>",
))
fig.update_layout(title="Corner handicap ROI by rating set (metric · window)", height=360,
                  xaxis=dict(tickformat=".0%", range=[0, bg["roi"].max() * 1.25]), yaxis=dict(title=None))
show(fig)
```

All `{python} n_combos` adjusted rating sets are profitable in the handicap market,
at `{python} f"{roi_lo:.1f}"`–`{python} f"{roi_hi:.1f}"`% ROI on
`{python} n_bets_lo`–`{python} n_bets_hi` bets each, after paying Pinnacle's margin.

**How the edge scales.** Raising the minimum disagreement before betting trades
volume for conviction. For the adj_nr / 19-game ratings:

```{python}
cv = load("ev_variant_peak_pnl_curves.csv")
cv = cv[cv["rule_family"] == "diff_sup"]
cv = cv[cv["n_bets"] >= 50]
peak = cv.loc[cv["total_pnl"].idxmax()]
breakeven = cv[cv["total_pnl"] > 0]["threshold"].min()

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, horizontal_spacing=0.1, subplot_titles=("Total profit (units)", "ROI"))
hover = "Edge ≥ %{x:.2f} corners<br>%{customdata[0]:,} bets<br>Profit %{customdata[1]:+.1f}u · ROI %{customdata[2]:.1%}<extra></extra>"
cd = cv[["n_bets", "total_pnl", "roi"]]
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=cv["threshold"], y=cv["total_pnl"], mode="lines", line=dict(color=ACCENT, width=2),
                         customdata=cd, hovertemplate=hover, showlegend=False), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=cv["threshold"], y=cv["roi"], mode="lines", line=dict(color=ACCENT, width=2),
                         customdata=cd, hovertemplate=hover, showlegend=False), row=1, col=2)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[peak["threshold"]], y=[peak["total_pnl"]], mode="markers+text",
                         marker=dict(color=ACCENT, size=9, line=dict(color="white", width=2)),
                         text=[f"peak {peak['total_pnl']:.0f}u at ≥{peak['threshold']:.2f}"], textposition="top right",
                         textfont=dict(color=TEXT_2, size=11), hoverinfo="skip", showlegend=False), row=1, col=1)
fig.update_xaxes(title="Minimum model–market disagreement (corners)")
fig.update_yaxes(tickformat=".0%", row=1, col=2)
fig.update_yaxes(zeroline=True, zerolinecolor=MUTED)
fig.update_layout(height=380)
fig.update_annotations(font=dict(size=13, color=TEXT_2))
show(fig)
```

Betting every match loses money: Pinnacle is sharp on average. Once the model
disagrees by `{python} f"{breakeven:.2f}"` corners or more, profit becomes positive. It peaks at
**`{python} f"{peak['total_pnl']:.0f}"` units** at a
`{python} f"{peak['threshold']:.2f}"`-corner threshold. ROI rises broadly as the
threshold tightens, which is the pattern you'd expect if the edge is real. Above about
1.2 corners it gets noisy, because there are only a few hundred bets left.
The 0.5 threshold used above was chosen on this same data, so treat the
peak as optimistic. The steady rise in ROI is the more reliable evidence.

**The totals market is different.** The same ratings were backtested against
Pinnacle's corner over/under lines, and every metric/window combination lost
money. My working hypothesis is that game state shifts *which side* wins the corners much more
than it changes *how many* corners there are in total, so correcting for it helps
the handicap market and doesn't help totals.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
This is a backtest over roughly two seasons on historical prices. Bets aren't
guaranteed to have been available at those odds or stakes, and results vary by
league: some are consistently profitable, others negative. See the
[methodology](methodology.qmd) page for caveats.
:::

## 9. Limitations and next steps

- **Match length is estimated.** The source data doesn't record stoppage time, so match length is
  taken as the later of 97 minutes and the last recorded event. Better data would
  improve the minute counts.
- **Other in-game factors aren't modelled yet.** Red cards and the *timing* of each game state (the
  effects grow as the match goes on) are obvious next adjustments.
- **Out-of-game factors aren't modelled either.** Manager changes, transfers and end-of-season motivation
  aren't captured beyond what the rolling window picks up.
- **No player-level data.** Lineup-aware ratings would help with injuries and rotation.
- **Data quality.** Some team names are split across different spellings in lower
  leagues, which affects rolling windows for the teams involved. Three leagues are
  excluded until they're given league/tier context.
- **Bet sizing.** All backtests use flat 1-unit stakes. Kelly-style sizing based on
  the size of the disagreement is untested.
